beats.care: It tests whether global courts can hold powerful leaders to account. It also shows how big powers push back when they disagree.
beats.what: The US froze the International Criminal Court's property in America and banned anyone from giving it money, goods or services.
beats.why: The US objects to the court's arrest warrant for Israel's prime minister and its Afghanistan probe, which could involve American troops.

cards.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on 9 Oct. Companies that serve the court could be penalised, with short exemptions for things like tech and pensions. Earlier US sanctions hit ICC officials; this time they target the court itself.

A court in The Hague that tries people, not countries, for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. It was set up by a treaty called the Rome Statute. The US, Israel and India never joined; most of Europe, Latin America and much of Africa did.
cards.title: what is the icc?

a.body: The court has no right to go after Americans or Israelis, since neither country joined it. Rubio warned the US will cut off the court unless it ends its 'threats'.
a.label: US says

b.body: The sanctions must be condemned and its work will go on. It urged member countries to step up their support.
b.label: ICC says

cards.body: Hours earlier, the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge of Indian Tamil descent who led a UN inquiry accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

cards.q: Should India join the International Criminal Court?

opts: Its cases target Israel's PM and could reach US troops
cards.q: Why is the US sanctioning the ICC?
cards.why: The US says the court shouldn't pursue citizens of countries that never joined it, like the US and Israel.

hook: The US just sanctioned a *whole court*. Why the ICC, and why now?
